class.name: PhysXFireSpread3D
class.brief_description: Fire that spreads over grass and leaf litter, with flames and smoke in NVIDIA Flow.
class.description: Burns the ground under it over a [member size] area, as wildfire models do (the WRF-SFIRE surface model): a fire front moves at Rothermel's rate of spread for the [member fuel_type], faster downwind and uphill, slowed by [member fuel_moisture] and stopped when the fuel is too wet. A fire in the wind grows into an ellipse whose length-to-width ratio follows the wind speed (Anderson 1983), as fire spread tools such as FARSITE draw it. Each patch of fuel burns down over a few seconds once the front reaches it. The heat it gives off drives a pool of emitters in a [PhysXFlow3D] of its own (or [member flow_path]), whose combustion draws the flames and smoke in raster and path tracing and lights the ground. Burnt ground turns black and the burning band glows through a [Decal], and the global shader parameters [code]fire_char_map[/code] (a [Texture2D], alpha: how burnt) and [code]fire_char_rect[/code] (world X and Z of the map's corner, and its size) let ground and vegetation shaders read the same map. Plants read [code]fire_state_map[/code] over the same rect (red: share of the fuel burnt, green: glow, blue: the peak flame length over 8 m, alpha: the peak crown scorch height over 24 m, from Van Wagner 1973): [GrassField3D] blades burn down to charred stubble, [PlantGenerator] plants char under the flame and scorch brown above it, and [TreeGenerator] bark chars to the flame length and leaves brown up to the scorch height. With [member spotting], burning fuel throws up glowing firebrands that the plume lofts and the wind carries; where one lands on unburnt fuel of any [PhysXFireSpread3D] it may start a spot fire ahead of the front. Water from a [PhysXParticleFluid3D] lying on the ground (a bucket, a hose, a burst tank) soaks the fuel under it: burning cells go out and the front stops at the wet ground ([method get_doused_cells]). With [member fire_whirls], strong flanks in a cross wind spin up whirls of flame that lift firebrands higher. With [member blowing_ash], a strong wind lifts the ash off the burnt ground as a drifting grey dust. Start a fire with [method ignite], or set [member heat_source] so that hot gas from another [PhysXFlow3D] (a campfire, a burning wreck) sets the ground alight.

method.name: get_ash_blown
method.description: Kilograms of ash the wind has lifted off the burnt ground so far ([member blowing_ash]).

method.name: get_fire_wind_at
method.description: The wind this fire draws in near the ground at [param position], in m/s (horizontal): its plume's indraft toward the burning front ([member fire_wind]). [method WorldFire.wind_at] sums it over every fire.

method.name: get_lee_whirls_spawned
method.description: How many of the fire whirls (see [method get_whirls_spawned]) formed on a lee slope and ran across it, spreading the fire sideways.

method.name: get_lightning_ignition_count
method.description: How many fires lightning has started in this grid.

method.name: lightning_ignition_chance
method.description: The chance (0..1) that a ground strike with [param continuing] seconds of continuing current lights fine fuel at [param moisture] (a fraction of its dry weight) whose moisture of extinction is [param extinction]: none under 40 ms of continuing current (Fuquay et al. 1972), rising to its full value by 0.2 s, times (1 - moisture / extinction) squared.

method.name: add_tree
method.description: Adds a tree or shrub the fire can light, standing at [param position], [param height] metres tall with its lowest foliage [param crown_base] metres up and a crown [param crown_radius] metres across its middle. Crowns from [member vegetation_field] are added by themselves.

method.name: clear_trees
method.description: Removes every tree, those from [member vegetation_field] and those added by [method add_tree].

method.name: extinguish
method.description: Puts the fire out. What has burnt stays charred.

method.name: get_burning_cells
method.description: Grid cells still flaming (more than 5% of their fuel left).

method.name: get_burnt_area
method.description: Square metres the fire has reached.

method.name: get_char_at
method.description: How burnt the ground at [param position] is: 0 unburnt, 1 burnt out.

method.name: get_crowns_burning
method.description: How many tree crowns are burning now.

method.name: get_crowns_lit
method.description: How many tree crowns have caught fire since the fire grid was built.

method.name: get_flame_length_at
method.description: The longest flame the front had at [param position], in metres (Byram's flame length from its fireline intensity). Plants under it are charred.

method.name: get_firebrand_count
method.description: Firebrands in the air now.

method.name: get_doused_cells
method.description: Burning cells put out so far by water from a [PhysXParticleFluid3D] (a bucket, a hose, a burst tank). Liquid water lying on the ground soaks the fine fuel under it; a burning cell whose fuel goes over the moisture of extinction goes out, and wet cells ahead of the front stop it.

method.name: get_flow
method.description: The [PhysXFlow3D] the flames are drawn in.

method.name: get_ground_height_at
method.description: The ground height the fire grid holds at [param position] (world Y), or the node's own height outside the grid.

method.name: get_spot_fire_count
method.description: Spot fires this node's firebrands have started so far.

method.name: get_heavy_fuel_at
method.description: Kilograms per square metre of large wood (logs and fallen branches from the [member vegetation_field]) left to burn at [param position].

method.name: get_intensity_at
method.description: Heat given off by the ground at [param position], in kW per square metre.

method.name: get_moisture_at
method.description: Dead fuel moisture at [param position], as a fraction of dry weight: [member fuel_moisture] as the weather has moved it, its patchiness, and the rain the fuel holds.

method.name: get_moisture_of_extinction
method.description: The fuel moisture (fraction of dry weight) at and above which the [member fuel_type] cannot burn.

method.name: get_scorch_height_at
method.description: The highest the fire's plume killed foliage at [param position], in metres: the crown scorch height of Van Wagner (1973) from the front's fireline intensity, the wind and the air temperature.

method.name: get_steam_mass
method.description: Kilograms of steam made so far where water met the fire: water from a [PhysXParticleFluid3D] on burning or glowing ground, and the front reaching standing or running water. Steam rises as a white cloud in a gas of its own, made only while something steams.

method.name: get_tree_burnt
method.description: The share of a tree's crown fuel burnt so far, 0 for a crown not lit; -1 past the last tree.

method.name: get_tree_count
method.description: How many trees the fire knows: crowns from [member vegetation_field] over its area and those added by [method add_tree].

method.name: get_whirl_count
method.description: How many fire whirls are spinning now (at most two).

method.name: get_whirls_spawned
method.description: How many fire whirls have formed since the fire started.

method.name: ignite
method.description: Sets the ground alight in a circle of [param radius] metres round [param position].

members.member: Wind over cold burnt ground lifts its ash as a low grey dust that drifts downwind, from about 4 m/s near the ground, in puffs as the gusts pass, until the ash is gone (a few minutes in a strong wind). Wet ground (rain, water) holds it. The burnt fine fuel leaves about 6% of its mass as ash, more under a burnt crown. See [method get_ash_blown].
Size of the fire grid's cells in metres. Smaller cells give a finer front and char edge, at more CPU time.
How fully burnt-out ground turns to black char.

If [code]true[/code], trees and shrubs catch fire from the ground fire under them (Van Wagner's crown fire initiation: the surface fire's intensity against the crown base height and the foliage's moisture), flare up and burn out in under a minute, light crowns their flame reaches, and throw many embers lofted by their own plume. Low crowns and shrubs catch easily, crowns high above the ground only scorch, and a dense stand carries fire from crown to crown where a sparse one does not.
When disabled, the fire stops where it is.

Strong fire on a flank that runs along the wind can spin up a fire whirl: a column of flame, some three flame lengths tall, that turns at about twice the fire's own updraft speed, wanders downwind and lofts firebrands higher. Whirls form most often when the wind is close to that updraft speed (Kuwana et al. 2008), last 10 to 30 seconds and die off the burning fuel. See [method get_whirl_count]. On a lee slope (steeper than about 20 degrees, falling away within 40 degrees of downwind, in a wind over 5.5 m/s) the ridge's eddy makes whirls too, whatever the fire's updraft; these run across the slope at about a fifth of the wind and light the fuel they pass, so the fire spreads sideways along the ridge (vorticity-driven lateral spread, Sharples et al. 2012).

The fire draws air in at the base of its plume: each stretch of burning front is a sink with an inflow of about half the fire's buoyant velocity just outside the flames (a few m/s at a strong front, as FireFlux measured), falling off with distance. Grass ([code]fire_wind_map[/code], [code]fire_wind_rect[/code]) and [PhysXCloth3D] lean into it through [method WorldFire.wind_at]. The spread takes only the pull of fire ahead of a front (another fire, a spot fire, the far side of a closing gap), so fronts draw together as they meet; a fire's pull on its own front is already in Rothermel's model.
Scales the fuel and heat the burning ground feeds into Flow.
The [PhysXFlow3D] to draw the flames in. Empty: one of its own, with 10 cm cells.

Moisture of conifer foliage as a fraction of its dry weight (1.0 is the 100% fire models assume); broadleaf foliage holds 1.6 times as much. Drier foliage (late summer drought, about 0.8) catches from weaker ground fires.
Scales the fuel's load (kilograms a square metre) from the [member fuel_type]: more fuel burns hotter, with taller flames.

Optional. Its red channel multiplies the fuel load over the area, so paths, rock and bare ground (black) stop the fire; its green channel adds moisture (1: 50% of dry weight more), so damp hollows and streamsides burn slowly or not at all.
Dead fuel moisture as a fraction of dry weight. Wetter fuel spreads slower; at the fuel's moisture of extinction (12% for short grass, 25% for tall grass and litter) it does not burn.

How unevenly the fuel lies: its load varies over a few metres and under a metre, with bare gaps, and damper patches hold more moisture, so the front runs unevenly and leaves a ragged scar with unburnt islands. 0: an even bed.
The fuel on the ground, with its load, depth and particle size from Anderson's fuel models.
Emission energy of the burning band and embers on the ground.
A [PhysXFlow3D] whose hot gas sets the ground under it alight where it is hotter than [member ignition_temperature]. Its [member PhysXFlow3D.cpu_readback] is turned on.
Temperature of the [member heat_source]'s gas, in its own units, that sets the ground alight.
Flame emitters at most: the flaming front is merged into tiles of about half a metre, and the strongest get one each, spread along the whole front.
Seconds the fuel takes to move most of the way (63%) to the moisture the air holds it at, with [member use_weather_moisture]: an hour for grass and fine litter. Shorten it for a game's pace.
The area that can burn, in metres along the node's X and Z, centred on it.

When enabled, what burns throws up firebrands (bark, twig and grass flakes of 2 to 10 mm): the fire's plume in its [PhysXFlow3D] lofts them, the wind at their height carries them, and they fall at their terminal velocity, which drops as they burn away (Tarifa et al. 1965, Tohidi et al. 2015). Grass throws few, litter more, burning logs the most. One that lands on unburnt fuel of any [PhysXFireSpread3D] starts a spot fire with Schroeder's (1969) probability of ignition for the fuel's moisture and the air temperature, so dry fuel in a strong wind catches ahead of the front and damp fuel does not. They show as short glowing streaks.
Scales how many firebrands the fire throws.
Speeds the fire up or slows it down, for a game's pace.

When enabled and a [WeatherMap3D] is active, the fuel moisture starts at [member fuel_moisture] and follows the weather: towards the equilibrium moisture of the air's temperature and humidity (Van Wagner and Pech 1985, as WRF-SFIRE takes it) over [member moisture_timelag], and wetted at once by rain the fuel intercepts. Burning ground that rain wets past the fuel's moisture of extinction goes out.

Storm lightning from a [WeatherLightning3D] can start fires: a ground strike in the grid with a long continuing current (over 40 ms) lights its cell with a chance that falls with the fuel's moisture towards the moisture of extinction (see [method lightning_ignition_chance]). Rain-soaked fuel does not take.
When enabled, the wind comes from the active [WeatherMap3D] where there is one; [member wind] is used otherwise.

Optional [VegetationField3D] the fuel follows: worn paths ([method VegetationField3D.get_path_passes_at]) are bare, leaf litter ([method VegetationField3D.get_litter_at]) adds fuel, and its logs and fallen branches ([method VegetationField3D.get_deadwood_at]) are large wood: a log catches from the fire burning under it unless too wet, flames for about Anderson's residence time (about 3 minutes per centimetre of diameter), then smoulders, glowing, for longer. Read when the grid is built.
The wind over the fire, in metres a second, when no weather map gives one.

constants.constant: Short grass (Anderson fuel model 1): fast, low flames.
Tall grass (fuel model 3): fast, tall flames.
Leaf and needle litter under trees (fuel models 8 and 9): slow, low flames that burn for longer.
